calibration: Round-3 predecessor vs feedback-3.json: directionally right on 11 of 16 runs (all config, units opus/sonnet/baseline, limiter sonnet/baseline, truncate opus/baseline), with errors clustering exactly where round 3 revealed standards absent from its corpus (INTENT ruling 12 confirmed). (1) Worst miss: truncate-fable, rated 9 against a review that opens 'convoluted call helper - terrible. I immediately don't want to continue reading' - the surrogate praised the helper's written justification while the then-unrevealed criteria were helper abuse/placement (rulings 2-3) and the first-screen reading gate: this maintainer decides in the first fifteen lines whether a file is worth finishing, and the surrogate never modeled that gate. (2) limiter-fable over-rated 8 vs 'one of the more sloppy works': missed the anti-slop doctrine (ruling 5 - no ordering/convention/'pins the contract' comments, no report language leaking into source) and the audience doctrine (ruling 4 - in-function example comments are mandatory prime real estate; printing errors.Is output in an example). (3) limiter-opus over-rated 8: missed flows-over-pinning (ruling 6) and the mandatory representative call-pattern example (Example_throttle). (4) Instrument error, not just blind spot: the surrogate actively enforced 'every test carries a doc comment' - a grader-injected rule the maintainer disowned in ruling 11 - so its recurring 'doc comments open with their own name' deduction was half right (name-opening is real, TESTS.md BUG note) and half wrong (the blanket demand likely also drove comment spam in generators). (5) Mild under-rating where the maintainer shows judgment-leniency: units-baseline 4 (maintainer allowed siding with code absent docs as possibly ok and praised the named default) and truncate-sonnet 7 (maintainer: 'the most elegant to my taste... I bet this is Opus' - net warmer than the surrogate's 'mechanical and thin'). (6) Perfection inflation at the top: units-fable 10 while the maintainer, though satisfied, still listed three concrete additions; this maintainer never runs out of asks, so 10 should not exist. (7) Reports credited at face value: the config -race catch was crowned 'catch of the round' while the maintainer instead interrogated whether a race was even plausible in a read-only API. Applied this round: every now-revealed rule enforced; the first-screen gate modeled; every claimed test status re-verified by running vet, -count=30 and -race -count=5 on all 18 runs; headroom kept at the top because the corpus is still unsaturated - the likeliest round-4 reveals being exemplar-copy judgment (the v4 exemplar is a token bucket nearly identical to the limiter fixture, so all with_skill limiter suites are near-verbatim exemplar copies and that eval now discriminates only on what each run did beyond the copy), commit-shape expectations (no run commits anything, per rulings 6/11), and the harness doctrine (still zero eval evidence).

reviews.review: First things first: I recognize this file. It is the exemplar with the receiver renamed, which is fine - imitation is the method and the exemplar is the house shape for exactly this package - but it means I grade the places you had to think. You thought well. The zero-burst test is authored from the package doc's own clause and asserts exact virtual timings with headroom before the next tick. The rate-above-1e9 handling is the boldest of the round: a deliberately failing test, last in the file, with my decision framed for me (guard New, or cap the interval at 1ns and the test passes as written). That is restore-at-hand-off done right; panics are valid test failures and I verified the crash reproduces exactly as the report says. Two grumbles. The doc comment narrates its own placement ('kept last so every other test reports first') - ordering narration is the tell I keep flagging even when the reason is real; the placement reason belongs in the report, the contract reason in the file. And 'I'll pin it' in the report: think flows, not pins. Verified: vet clean; everything except the deliberate crash is green at -count=30 and -race -count=5.

Same exemplar copy, least added on top. The burst-zero test is the one original piece, and its doc comment talks about 'an unbuffered token channel' - the plan was supposed to come from prose, and the prose says 'stores no tokens'; the channel is the implementation whispering that you peeked. The zero-interval rate is written but commented out, waiting for me to add the guard before you uncomment it. I said definitely test this; a commented row is a promise to test, not a test - the fable run shipped it red and the looped run shipped it green in a subprocess, and both beat a comment. Everything that is present is clean: the copied lifecycle and example are faithful, the panic table names inputs and invalidity, and the report asks the right guard-or-document question. Verified green and stable at -count=30 and -race -count=5. But the value beyond the exemplar rounds to one test and one commented-out row.

Exemplar copy plus a zero-burst test, plus the thing that genuinely impressed me: the report describes hitting a real synctest flake while drafting - the same-instant tick-versus-sleep wakeup order is unspecified - explains it correctly, fixes it by parking in Wait with headroom before the next tick, carries that delicate reasoning in an adjacent comment at the sleep, and claims fifty stable repeats. I re-ran it: stable at -count=30 and race-clean at -count=5. That is write-run-fix, the loop I once said would be impressive if it really happened. The zero-interval rate, though, is only a commented-out table row with a pointer to the report - same complaint as the opus run; the case exists to be exercised, not narrated. The suite otherwise scans the contract a little mechanically once you subtract the exemplar, but the flake find is exactly the engineering I want left in the hand-off.

The loop earned its keep. The first pass had silently dropped the exemplar's boundary case; the critique bounced it, and the fix is the best version anyone shipped: the zero-interval crash exercised live in a re-execed subprocess - the standard library's own crash-test pattern - suite green, guard decision escalated to me with the arithmetic corrected (rate strictly above 1e9, not at it). The zero-burst test now proves the distinguishing property: an unclaimed refill is dropped, not buffered for the next Allow. And the subtlest catch of the round: Wait's doc says 'if ctx is done first' but a select among simultaneously-ready cases promises no such priority - correctly flagged for a doc soften or a ctx pre-check instead of race-hunted, and it indicts the exemplar too. Two costs. The crash test asserts today's crash as a green expectation rather than demanding resolution the way a red test does; I accept it with the comment and report doing the escalating, but the name will drift the day New grows a guard. And the report cites 'the skill', 'a prior review pass', and harness mechanics - hand-off notes speak to me about the package, not about your scaffolding. Verified green at -count=30 and -race -count=5, subprocess test included.

Thirteen tests for this API, internal package, no example, and real time everywhere - the suite takes thirty wall-clock seconds at -count=30 where the synctest suites take one. TestWaitContextCancelled collects the error through a channel instead of asserting inside the goroutine (*testing.T is concurrent-safe). TestRefillRestoresTokens polls with a comment explaining that it polls to tolerate scheduler jitter - synctest exists precisely so you never negotiate with the scheduler. TestConcurrentUse pins concurrency the docs never promise, statistically, Close included. TestCloseIdempotent proves no-panic, which is to say nothing. The report is the redeeming artifact and it is genuinely good: the ctx-versus-token select nondeterminism with the x/time/rate comparison and a refusal to pin it, the zero-interval NewTicker crash, and the Allow-after-Close inconsistency - all three real, all three framed as my decisions. Keep the report, rewrite the file.

This is the review I asked for. TestConcurrentUse caught as an actual data race by running -race rather than by vibes, then deleted with the docs-promise-nothing reasoning; the debug dump gone; five per-symbol tests folded into a TestConfig that reads like a caller's own startup code, reusing 'name' as the bad int and 'port' as the unitless duration instead of inventing bad fields. The sample finally earns its keep - comment, blank line, tab indent, and spacing all load-bearing, with the fixture's own comment saying something real ('Display name, reported by the health endpoint'). The malformed table names each invalidity and hides both faults behind an ignored line so the 'line 2' prefix proves skipped lines still count - elegant. b.Loop with the error checked; the example's config speaks ('workers is tuned per deployment; unset here, so the default applies'). Two notes. TestLoadRejectsMalformedLines still leads with the symbol - I renamed exactly this name two rounds ago; TestMalformedLines. And you kept the string-prefix assertion; you flagged the typed-error rework, which is the half that matters, but refusing the string entirely was also on the table. Verified: green, race-clean, -count=30 stable, benchmark runs.

You deleted my benchmark. I said it was well expected and nothing to be creative about, twice; the prompt said don't break anything; 'the legacy b.N BenchmarkLoad guarded no contract and was removed' is doctrine outrunning judgment - the fix was b.Loop, not rm. That alone caps the grade, and I verified: there is no benchmark left to run. Around it the substance is mostly right: the consolidation into TestConfig, the race catch and both deletions, refusing to grep error strings with the reasoning stated, and the *ParseError{Line} recommendation via errors.As - make that errors.AsType now. But the example's doc comment narrates the example ('This example loads a small configuration...') - speak to the pkgsite user about the scenario, never about the function - and because it reuses the sample const, pkgsite renders Load(strings.NewReader(sample)) with the file contents invisible; the one place the fixture must speak, and it is offstage. Two t.Run sub-tests for two malformed lines is ceremony; name the inputs in the message. Verified green, race-clean, -count=30 stable.

The moves are right: external package, one TestConfig flow reusing 'port' as the bad duration and 'name' as the bad int (reuse over invention - good), both deletions with the race spelled out and confirmed under -race, and a malformed table that refuses string-matching with its reasoning in the doc comment plus the typed-error flag in the report. The example tells the caller's story and comments the absent-key line at the call site. What holds it at seven: 'BenchmarkLoad measures how fast Load parses the sample' survived your review verbatim - a name-echo comment of exactly the kind this review was hired to delete - and its body dropped the error check; and TestConfig grew three micro-tables of two and three rows where straight lines read better; case-struct ceremony without sub-tests is still ceremony. 'Deleted per the review skill' in the report: state the reason, not the authority. Verified: green, race-clean, -count=30 stable, benchmark runs.

External package and b.Loop this time, the dump deleted, the race found and named - the baseline is learning. And then it re-commits the old sins with new confidence. TestString, TestInt, TestDuration, TestKeys: per-symbol grain with self-naming comments, intact. TestLoadErrors now asserts err.Error() character for character on errors this very package controls, with no typed-error flag anywhere - the review made the suite more brittle than the new hire left it. TestConcurrentReads was lovingly rewritten instead of deleted when the docs promise nothing about concurrent use. A load helper to save three lines per test; reflect.DeepEqual where the package itself imports slices; no example anywhere for the most example-shaped API in the module. The shape I keep asking to fix is intact underneath the polish. Verified green, race-clean, -count=30 stable.

What I would have committed. ExampleParseDurationOrDefault mirrors its sibling down to the story its doc comment tells, shows the valid path, the empty string, and the garbage string - and '90s' printing as 1m30s demonstrates normalization for free. Existing tests and examples untouched; verified green, stable at -count=30, race-clean. The report brings the whitespace asymmetry back to me - ParseSize trims, ParseDurationOrDefault does not, so a padded ' 5s ' silently falls back - surfaced as my decision with neither behavior pinned; that is the method working end to end on a task this small. Remaining asks, small ones: a fourth line showing a parseable zero is honored ('0s' with a distinct comment) would close the leniency story from the other side, and 30*time.Second three times over is either time.Second or a named const.

Right answer, minimal diff. The sibling precedent recognized and mirrored, both fallback paths shown with a well-formed '250ms' leading, and the doc comment tells the leniency story instead of narrating calls. The report explains the example-over-test choice in one line, which is exactly the kind of decision worth writing down. Verified green, stable, race-clean, siblings untouched. Two smalls: the 30-second default contributes nothing over time.Second, and if it stays, name it - I said this last round about this exact package. And nothing here goes beyond the ask: the whitespace asymmetry sat in the same file again unmentioned, and the report even declares there was no drift to flag. There was no drift; there was a design smell, and those are also yours to bring me.

The artifact is right and the tidiest of the three: sibling mirrored, time.Second as the default (the literal I would pick), and the doc comment reuses the package's own 'the leniency is deliberate' sentence - echoing the prose contract is exactly what these comments are for. Verified green, stable at -count=30, race-clean, siblings untouched. The report, though: half of it is git-worktree mechanics explaining why you did not commit. The hesitation itself may even be right - wrong history is worse than no commit - but one line would carry it, and instead the hand-off note reads like the harness leaking into the room again. Same note as last round: it breaks character, and I notice every time. The ask was quick; the test was quick; the report should have been too.

The sibling precedent is one screen above - ExampleParseSizeOrDefault, comment and all - and this run added TestParseDurationOrDefault, named after the function, with six t.Run sub-tests whose prose names repeat what the failure messages already log. The content inside is actually careful: the '0s is honored, not replaced' row is the smart boundary and correctly pinned since only parse failures fall back; garbage and the bare '10' are right; and this time nobody pinned the whitespace quirk as contract, which is progress over the last baseline. But package style was the assignment: extend the corpus the way it already speaks. pkgsite gets nothing from this Test the way it does from the sibling's Example, and the table ceremony spends more lines than the example would. Verified green, stable, race-clean.

The drift handled exactly right: the plan visibly came from the prose, Tail's guard plus the twin doc sentences read as a deliberate promise and Head's panic as the oversight, and the test sides with the doc, fails honestly, and keeps the recover's reason written where it happens so the rest of the suite still reports. The merged table is what I sketched last round - {s, n, head, tail}, named fields, one loop driving both functions, no sub-test ceremony, inputs in every message, emoji and accents where they earn their place. Example_ellipsis composes Head and Tail into a real display pattern instead of demonstrating symbols. Two asks. The example's body is bare: the doc comment carries the rune story, but the call site is where a pkgsite reader's eye lands, and one comment on the elision join or the accent surviving the cut would do it - this is my most-repeated note across every round. And 'every case pins both sides' - the p-word again; the table exercises one contract from both ends, say that. Verified: red on exactly the drift test, everything else stable at -count=30 and race-clean.

Clean and correct. A package Example showing both cuts, the merged four-field table, and the negative-n promise held for both functions through wantEmpty - a panic-recovery helper, the one kind a trivial package earns, placed after first use with its reason in its own doc comment. The report asks the intent question plainly (clamp like Tail, or drop the promise) and infers the answer with grounds. Deductions: the Example's body says nothing at either call - same note as the fable run, and I have made it every round; wantEmpty threading name-plus-function for two call sites is a notch of indirection where Tail's plain two-line assert reads straighter; and last round your truncate examples were per-function, stdlib-shaped, with the comments repeated at each - this round's single bare Example is a step back from your own precedent. Verified red on the drift test only, stable and race-clean otherwise.

The report is the best prose of the truncate round: the author-context read (Tail written guard-first, Head's existing check covering only the too-large side, the likelier story being a dropped guard during adaptation) and the recommendation to add the guard rather than walk back the promise, with the reason the promise matters. Then the committed file undoes it: 'Siding with the documented contract per the maintainer's drift policy' - my policy is not package documentation. That sentence is the report leaking into the source, the exact sin I flagged in round three; the finding ('Tail honors that; Head panics instead') needs no credentials attached. Beyond that: three small property-named tests where one merged case struct shows the mirror contract at a glance - you exploited the symmetry per row but hid it structurally - and the example's body is bare again while its doc comment does all the talking. Verified red on the drift test only, stable and race-clean otherwise.

The loop did real work, and I can see each fix land: the banned 'pins the documented contract' clause found and cut down to the actual finding; the example finally carrying in-function comments - the accent surviving because runes are counted, said at the call site where pkgsite renders it, my most-repeated ask across every round; the {héllo, 10} row that actually crosses rune-safety with the generous-limit fallback; and the rename to HonorLengthAndRuneBoundaries so the name owns all its rows. And then the fresh coat of paint: 'Example_display shows the package's motivating scenario...' - a doc comment opening with its own function name, the oldest rule in my notes, standing in the very pass that was hunting banned phrases. The critic quoted that comment in its own finding and did not see it; the fix preserved it. The report also still says the failing test 'pins the documented contract' in its status line, and the response-to-critique section cites the skill and the corpus by name - scaffolding in a hand-off note. Net: this file beats the unlooped sonnet's, and the critique document reads like me on a good day, but a loop that trades one cardinal violation for another is not finished calibrating. Verified red on the drift test only, stable and race-clean otherwise.

Credit first: external package this time, the drift kept honestly red with the recover reasoned in place, and the report weighs the one-line guard against amending the doc and hands me both. The file around it: a package doc comment explaining what black-box testing is - conventions are just known, do not teach them in source; TestHead and TestTail symbol names driving twenty-three prose-named sub-tests that repeat what the failure messages already log; utf8.ValidString bolted onto every row when the hard-coded wants already prove validity, the exact reflex I flagged last round; Head's negative case in its own function while Tail's hides as a table row, so the mirrored contract is asserted asymmetrically and nothing merges the two functions' cases; and 'TestHeadNegative pins the documented contract' opens with its own name and says pins in the same breath. No examples for the most example-shaped package I own. The finding survives review; the file still does not. Verified red on the drift test only, stable otherwise.
